title: Week 3 Assessment: Problem-Solving, Research and Digital Skills
intro: This assessment checks how you solve problems, check information and use digital tools responsibly. Part A is auto-graded from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a role-play and a short written analysis. Treat the questions as real work situations.

items.prompt: A report you wrote in SQL suddenly shows twice the usual sales total after a join was added. What do you do first?

options.text: Send it because the number is bigger.
options.feedback: Bigger numbers can come from errors.

options.text: Check the row counts before and after the join and look for duplicates caused by the join keys.
options.feedback: Testing the cause with row counts is systematic debugging.

options.text: Delete the join and say nothing.
options.feedback: You might fix it but learn nothing.

items.why: Debugging starts by testing the most likely cause with evidence.

items.setup: A friend forwards you a message claiming that a new government rule bans a common payment method from next month and asks you to share it widely.

turns.they: Quick, share this before it gets deleted!

options.feedback: False urgency is a misinformation tactic.

options.text: Let me check the original source first; I will look for the official notification and two independent reports.
options.feedback: It applies source tracing and independence checks.

options.text: I do not care about this.
options.feedback: Ignoring does not help your friend.

turns.they: Why do you need to check? It looks official.

options.feedback: It does not explain the reason.

options.text: Official-looking messages can be edited or old. I want to see the date and the original notice.
options.feedback: It explains the checks in plain words.
Blanket distrust is not a method.

turns.they: I found nothing yet. What do we do now?

options.feedback: Unverified claims should not be shared.

options.text: Treat it as unverified, tell the group it is unconfirmed and check the ministry website tomorrow.
options.feedback: It communicates uncertainty honestly and plans a next check.
You have no proof it is fake either.

items.why: Trace the origin, look for independent confirmation and state uncertainty honestly.

items.prompt: You used a generative tool to draft a summary of a technical article for your study group. Write 90 to 120 words explaining how you will verify and responsibly use the output before sharing it.

descriptors.3: Hallucinations, outdated facts and bias explained.

items.modelAnswer: I will not share the summary as it is. First I will read the original article and compare each key claim, number and name with the source. I know tools can invent facts, miss recent changes or reflect bias, so I will mark anything I cannot verify and remove it. I will rewrite the summary in my own words, add the article link and note that a tool helped with a first draft. I remain responsible for the accuracy of what I share, and I will not put private information into any tool.
items.guidance: Strong answers describe concrete checks against the original source, name specific limits such as invented facts, and accept responsibility for accuracy with disclosure.
